text:
# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization is a family of techniques that reduce the rendering load of voxel-based scenes by reconstructing geometry from triangles and removing sides adjacent to solid neighbors, thereby avoiding the rendering of hidden faces [S1, unofficial]. It solves the problem of naively rendering all 6 faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, by exposing only faces adjacent to empty space or out-of-bounds [S2, unofficial]. Unlike sibling methods that perform fine-grained face-by-face culling based on neighbor occupancy [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md), this family encompasses broader visibility strategies including camera-relative checks [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md), [multi-view projection](#5937-multi-view-projection.md) consistency [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md), and opacity-based filtering [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md).

## Shared principles
The core mechanism across this family is the identification and exclusion of geometric primitives that do not contribute to the final image. This is achieved through three primary categories of checks:

1.  **Topological Culling:** Determining visibility based on the occupancy of adjacent voxels. A face is culled if the neighbor in the direction of the face normal is solid [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial]. This is the most common form, used in basic mesh generation [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) and dynamic updates [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md).
2.  **View-Relative Culling:** Determining visibility based on the camera's position and orientation. This includes back-face culling (dot product of normal and view direction) [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md), camera-space orientation checks [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md), and multi-view projection consistency [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md).
3.  **Attribute-Based Culling:** Determining visibility based on material properties or precomputed visibility masks. This includes opacity thresholds [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md), coverage masks for partial shapes [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md), and buried block bitmasks [[Buried Bitmask Optimization](#3960-buried-bitmask-optimization.md)].

All methods aim to reduce the number of triangles sent to the rasterizer, thereby improving performance. The specific implementation varies from simple neighbor lookups to complex GPU-based projection tests.

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)
A technique for dynamically updating a voxel chunk's internal state and face visibility when blocks are placed or removed, using neighbor checks to toggle shared faces without regenerating the entire mesh. It differs from its sibling [Greedy face merging](8935-greedy-face-merging.md) by maintaining per-block visibility flags rather than merging adjacent quads into larger primitives, and from [Blocky meshing](31-blocky-meshing.md) generally by focusing on incremental state updates rather than batch mesh generation.

### [Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration](2176-voxel-block-shape-culling-configuration.md)
A trait-based system that defines block geometry, transparency culling modes, and lighting per block type to optimize mesh generation. It solves the problem of managing diverse voxel behaviors (opaque, transparent, fluid, complex shapes) by decoupling shape definition from the meshing algorithm. Unlike sibling methods that rely on global boolean flags or simple neighbor checks, this approach assigns specific `CullMode` and `Shape` traits to individual block IDs, allowing for nuanced handling such as merging transparent faces or generating non-cubic geometry.

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
A method for optimizing blocky mesh generation by representing the geometric coverage of a voxel face as a bit mask, allowing for the culling of partially occluded faces from partial shapes (such as stairs and slabs). Unlike basic neighbor checks that treat faces as binary solid/empty, this method solves the problem where a boolean solid flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face. It sets itself apart from [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) by enabling fine-grained visibility decisions based on geometric overlap rather than simple adjacency, and from [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) by separating geometric coverage from material transparency properties.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
A dynamic mesh generation and buffer management technique for voxel terrain that packs vertex attributes into compact 32-bit integers and manages incremental mesh updates via a free-list allocator. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and frequent GPU buffer reallocations in dynamic voxel environments by storing position, texture, lighting, and texture coordinates in two `uint32` values per vertex, and by reusing deleted vertex slots to maintain a dense, contiguous vertex array. It differs from static meshing methods by supporting real-time addition and removal of blocks with immediate neighbor [face culling](#8735-face-culling.md) and buffer synchronization.

### [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md)
A geometry shader-based optimization that rejects invisible faces in voxel rendering by determining front/back orientation in projection space and masking faces shared between neighboring voxels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by performing visibility checks per-voxel within the [geometry shader](#4369-geometry-shader-quads.md) using projection-space dot products, rather than pre-computing chunk-level masks or using ray-casting for visibility.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
A coarse-grained optimization method that determines which voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering based on the camera's position and orientation, avoiding unnecessary geometry generation when the viewing context has not changed significantly. It operates by comparing the camera's integer block coordinates and primary viewing direction against the previous frame's values to skip index updates, or by evaluating the dot product between surface normals and the view direction to cull invisible faces. Unlike sibling methods that perform fine-grained face-by-face culling based on neighbor occupancy, this method focuses on block-level visibility decisions driven by camera movement and orientation.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
[Extraction of Surface Points](#5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md) is a fast display method for direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It solves the problem of rendering speed in volume visualization by converting the volume into a sparse list of surface points rather than a dense mesh or ray-cast image. It differs from its siblings, which typically generate polygonal meshes (e.g., [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md)) or use [ray-marching](#6739-ray-marching.md), by projecting discrete voxel samples directly onto the image plane.

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
[Mask Projection Culling](#6836-mask-projection-culling.md) is a visibility-based mesh filtering technique that removes faces and vertices not consistently observed across multiple camera poses by projecting points into camera space and comparing their depth against rendered depth maps or binary masks. It differs from neighbor-occupancy checks [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) by relying on external camera viewpoints rather than local voxel topology, and from simple back-face culling [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md) by handling complex occlusions and non-convex geometries through multi-view consistency.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
This method removes geometric artifacts and occluded regions from a 3D mesh by projecting its vertices into multiple camera views and comparing against reference depth maps. It classifies faces as "seen" (visible in at least 20 views), "unseen" (occluded or background), or "forecast" (distant potential geometry). It is distinct from neighbor-based culling (e.g., [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)) because it relies on multi-view consistency rather than local voxel occupancy, making it suitable for unbounded or non-volumetric meshes like those from [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md).

### [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)
Face Culling is a mesh generation optimization that prevents rendering block faces occluded by adjacent solid voxels, significantly reducing triangle count in homogeneous voxel terrain. It solves the problem of naively rendering all 6 faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, by exposing only faces adjacent to empty space or out-of-bounds. Unlike [Voxel Block Placement with Face Culling](923-voxel-block-placement-with-face-culling.md) which may handle placement logic, or [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) which uses coverage masks, this method relies on direct neighbor occupancy checks during [mesh construction](#1022-isosurface-point-indexing-and-mesh-assembly.md).

### [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md)
[Opacity-based Mesh Culling](#8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) is a post-processing [optimization technique](#7922-optimization-technique.md) applied to polygonal meshes extracted from [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) or volumetric representations. It solves the problem of excessive mesh complexity and storage overhead by discarding geometric primitives that contribute negligible visual information. Unlike sibling methods that rely on spatial occupancy or block visibility [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md), this method evaluates the radiometric contribution (opacity) of individual faces or triangles, retaining only those that meet a minimum opacity threshold. This results in a significant reduction in mesh count while preserving visual fidelity.

### [From-Region Visibility Preprocessing](9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md)
[From-region visibility preprocessing](#9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md) is a technique that precomputes which geometric primitives are visible from specific regions of a scene to optimize rendering performance. It solves the problem of redundant rendering of occluded geometry by determining visibility sets for spatial regions in advance. It differs from sibling methods like [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) which operate on local voxel adjacency, by operating on global or semi-global geometric occlusion relationships.

### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The process resets the buried bitmask for the chunk, creates mapped adjacent chunks for neighbor access, and iterates through all blocks to determine if they are buried via `block->isBuried(...)`. If all blocks in a chunk are buried, the mesh is marked empty and generation is skipped. During mesh generation, any block that is air or has its buried flag set is skipped [S2, unofficial].

### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw, by generating opaque faces between air/transparent blocks and transparent faces only for blocks touching air [S3, unofficial]. The first pass generates opaque faces, testing for opaque blocks if transparent blocks exist in the chunk (ignoring transparent and air), otherwise testing for non-air. The second pass tests for non-air blocks to mark only transparent blocks, generating faces for transparent blocks touching air but not adding faces between transparent and solid blocks. Solid block types are filtered out during the transparent pass before constructing AO values [S3, unofficial].

### Smart Leaf Rendering
A leaf block rendering strategy that preserves alpha cutouts on outer leaf surfaces while culling internal faces to reduce vertex count [S4, unofficial]. It is controlled by a global static enum `sLeafRenderMode`, which defaults to `ChunkRenderer::LeafRenderMode::Smart` [S4, unofficial].

### Hidden Face Extension
A proposed optimization where the 2D grid includes a 'don't care' state (2) to allow rectangles to extend into hidden areas, potentially reducing total rectangle count [S5, unofficial]. While this might reduce mesh size, it increases the load on the rasterizer [S5, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of removing interior polygons was introduced in early [voxel terrain generation](#4140-chunk-based-voxel-terrain-generation.md) implementations to improve rendering performance [S1, unofficial]. The original motivation was that brute-force instantiation of cube models resulted in the engine needlessly rendering 12 triangles (6 sides) when only 2 triangles (1 side) were visible [S1, unofficial]. To address this, a class was added to reconstruct cubes from triangles and check for solid neighbors, preventing the rendering of sides adjacent to those neighbors [S1, unofficial]. This optimization was further enhanced by combining the meshes of all individual cubes into a single big mesh called a 'chunk' [S1, unofficial].
